widget.instructions: The board shows the force on the car during the collision. Its third-law partner acts on the truck.

args.text: Third-law forces are equal in size whatever the masses.

stem: A {{M}} kg truck and a {{m}} kg car collide head-on. At one instant the truck pushes on the car with a force of {{F}} N.
At that instant, how large is the force the car exerts on the truck?

hints.text: The two forces are one interaction between the truck and the car.
Newton's third law doesn't depend on mass or on who is 'stronger'. The masses change the accelerations, not the forces.
The car pushes back on the truck with an equal force in the opposite direction.

heavier-pushes-harder.text: The masses don't change the size of a third-law pair. They change the accelerations: the car accelerates more because it is lighter.

third-law-forces-cancel.text: The two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other. Each one changes the motion of the body it acts on.

generic.text: Use Newton's third law: equal in size, opposite in direction, on the other body.

workedSolution.text: The truck pushing the car and the car pushing the truck are a third-law pair.
So the car pushes on the truck with {{F}} N, backwards. The car's acceleration is {{F}} ÷ {{m}} = {{ac}} m/s²; the truck's only {{F}} ÷ {{M}} = {{at}} m/s².

heavier-pushes-harder.front: In a truck–car collision, which pushes harder on the other?
heavier-pushes-harder.back: Neither: the forces are equal and opposite. The car accelerates more because it is lighter.

third-law-forces-cancel.front: Do the two forces of a third-law pair cancel?
third-law-forces-cancel.back: No. They act on different bodies.

generic.back: Equal and opposite forces on the two bodies, whatever their masses.

accessibility.altText: The car with the truck's push on it drawn as one arrow.
accessibility.nonDragAlternative: The board only illustrates the force; type your answer in the box.
